summary: An early Telnet option, written in 1974, that lets two sides negotiate how a remote system handles horizontal tab stops on output. It is one of a family of small options by the same author covering how a terminal's output formatting is handled. It is historic and no longer used in practice.

eli5.summary: Old computer terminals could jump to the next tab stop, like a typewriter. This note lets two computers agree on where those stops are, so text lines up right.

subtitle: Negotiating horizontal tab stops on a Telnet connection.

tldr.problem: When a remote system sends text over Telnet with tab characters, the two sides need to agree on where the tab stops are (the column positions where a tab should land).
tldr.mechanism: This option defines commands that let the sender and receiver negotiate: either party can propose who should handle tabs and what the stop positions should be. They exchange messages with stop position values and reach agreement.
tldr.outcome: Both sides know which party controls tab stops and where they are set. The RFC is Historic and no longer used; modern systems use fixed tab widths or ignore tabs.

today: RFC 653 is Historic and has not been updated. The option is no longer used in practice; modern Telnet and terminal applications use fixed tab widths (typically 8 characters) or do not support tabs at all.

sections.title: The Telnet Tab Stop Negotiation Option
sections.content:
RFC 653 defines the NAOHTS option (Negotiate About Output Horizontal Tabstops), a Telnet option for handling tab stops on output. Telnet is a protocol for remote terminal access where one computer sends text to another. When that text contains a tab character (a control character that jumps the cursor), both computers need to know where the tab stops are—the column numbers where the cursor lands.

Before this option was negotiated, systems had no standard way to agree on tab positions. This RFC solves that by letting the two sides exchange messages about which party controls tab stops and what positions to use.
sections.eli5: Old terminals jump the cursor to set columns when they see a Tab. This option lets two computers agree on which columns those are.

sections.title: How the Negotiation Works
sections.content:
The negotiation uses the standard Telnet option protocol. One side sends IAC DO NAOHTS (asking to negotiate), and the other replies with IAC WILL NAOHTS (agreeing) or IAC WON'T NAOHTS (refusing). After agreement, the sides use IAC SB (subnegotiation) messages to exchange details. The data sender uses DS (code 1) and the data receiver uses DR (code 0) to specify what it wants: zero means "I will handle it"; values 1 to 250 specify tab stop column numbers; 255 means "you handle it and decide the stops yourself."

The guiding rule is simple: if both sides want to handle tabs, the sender wins (because the sender knows the data format). If neither wants to, the receiver must do it.
sections.eli5: The two computers say "do you want to handle this?" "Yes." Then they say "here are the stop positions" with numbers. They pick who handles it by a simple rule: if both want to, the sender wins.

sections.title: Using the Option
sections.content: Once negotiated, the chosen party (sender or receiver) understands where the tab stops are on the other end. When a tab character arrives, the receiver applies it correctly: the cursor jumps to the next column in the list of stops provided during negotiation. The two sides can also propose different arrangements at any time, allowing them to adapt if terminal settings change or a new process starts.
sections.eli5: After agreement, when a Tab arrives, the receiver jumps the cursor to the right column. Either side can change the agreement later if something changes.
